title: I have a headache
title_target: Με πονάει το κεφάλι — Meh poh-nah-ee toh keh-fah-lee
goal: Explain what's wrong at the pharmacy or the clinic — using a pattern that, once again, makes your body part the subject and you the target.
bekal: use με πονάει and πονάει το … μου
name symptoms: fever, cough, a cold
ask for medicine at the pharmacy

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — At the ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ
dialogs.intro: Greek pharmacies are marked by a glowing green cross, and pharmacists can give many medicines without a prescription — they're the first stop for Greeks with a minor illness. Ana walks in early in the morning.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Not so well. I have a headache.
lines.literal: not — I-am — very — well. me (obj) — it-hurts — the — head — my.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: A little. And my throat hurts.
lines.literal: a-little. and — me (obj) — it-hurts — the — throat — my.

lines.speaker: Φαρμακοποιός:
lines.id: How many days have you been like this?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Two days. I can't sleep well.

lines.speaker: Φαρμακοποιός:
lines.id: Take these pills, twice a day, after meals.
lines.literal: take — these (n pl) — the — pills, two — times — the — day, after — the — food.

lines.speaker: Φαρμακοποιός:
lines.id: No. And drink plenty of water. If it goes on, see a doctor.
lines.literal: no. and — drink — much — water. if — it-continues, go — to-the — doctor.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Thank you. How much is it?

notes: ⚠️ **"I have a headache" in Greek is "the head hurts me".** *Με πονάει το κεφάλι μου.* The body part is the **subject**, you are the **target**. It's the same pattern as μου αρέσει from the last unit — and once you see the pattern repeat, it stops feeling strange.

**There are two equally correct ways**: *Με πονάει το κεφάλι* and *Πονάει το κεφάλι μου*. The first uses **με** (me as target), the second **μου** (the head of mine). In conversation they're often combined: *Με πονάει το κεφάλι μου* — technically doubled up, but that's what people really say.
⚠️ **Πονάει for one part, πονάνε for several.** *Με πονάει το πόδι μου* (my foot hurts) but *Με πονάνε τα πόδια μου* (my feet hurt). The verb follows the body part, not you.

**Έχω is used for symptoms you can "have"**: έχω πυρετό (fever), έχω βήχα (cough), έχω γρίπη (flu), έχω αλλεργία (allergy). Pain uses πονάει. ⚠️ Telling them apart is easier than it looks: if English says "it hurts" or "-ache", use πονάει; if English says "I have…", use έχω.
**Είμαι άρρωστος / άρρωστη** = "I'm sick", a general statement. The ending follows your own gender: men say **άρρωστος**, women **άρρωστη**. The same goes for *κουρασμένος / κουρασμένη*.

**Πάρτε, πιείτε, πηγαίνετε are polite commands** — just the εσείς form with a commanding tone, and exactly what pharmacists, doctors, and officials use. The casual form drops -τε: *πάρε*, *πιες*, *πήγαινε*. ⚠️ Commands in Greek don't sound rude at all; they're the standard way to give advice and directions.

**Περαστικά!** (*peh-rah-stee-KAH*) literally "may it pass", is said to anyone who's ill — by the pharmacist, the neighbor, the taxi driver, anyone. It's one of the warmest words you can offer. The reply is simply **Ευχαριστώ**.
**Χρειάζομαι** (*khree-AH-zoh-meh*, "I need") ends in -ομαι but means something entirely ordinary — another reminder that the group isn't the passive. *Χρειάζομαι βοήθεια.* — I need help.

grammars.title: Saying what hurts
body: Three patterns, and you'll hear all three. Pick one to use yourself and recognize the other two.
after: **The little words are the ones from unit 17**, just in the ordinary object form: **με, σε, τον/την, μας, σας, τους**. *Τον πονάει το στομάχι του.* — His stomach hurts.
⚠️ **Πονάω can also be used with no object**, meaning "I'm in pain" in general: *Πονάω πολύ.* A useful short sentence when there's no time to say where.

grammars.title: Symptoms and requests at the pharmacy
body: Two opening verbs — έχω and χρειάζομαι — cover nearly everything you need.
after: **Emergency numbers in Greece: 112** for everything, **166** for an ambulance. Sentences that should come out without thinking: **Χρειάζομαι γιατρό!** (I need a doctor) and **Βοήθεια!** (*voh-EE-thyah*, help!).

⚠️ **Greek pharmacies take turns staying open.** Closed ones post a list of **εφημερεύοντα φαρμακεία** — the pharmacies on duty that night — on the door. Look for those words if you need medicine at midnight.

blocks.title: Body parts you already know from English
items: **η καρδιά** heart → *cardiology*, *cardiovascular*. **το στομάχι** stomach → *stomatitis* via στόμα (mouth). **το δέρμα** skin → *dermatology*. **το αίμα** blood → *anemia*, *hemoglobin*.
**ο εγκέφαλος** brain → *encephalitis*. **ο οφθαλμός** eye (medical term) → *ophthalmology*. **το οστό** bone → *osteoporosis*. **ο πνεύμονας** lung → *pneumonia*.

⚠️ Everyday Greek uses **different** words from the medical terms: people say *μάτι*, not *οφθαλμός*, and *καρδιά*, not *καρδία*. So English medical vocabulary teaches you the formal layer — useful at the hospital, not in conversation.
**Περαστικά!** and **Σιδερένιος!** (*see-dheh-REH-nyohs*, "be strong as iron") both mean get well soon. The second is for someone who has just had surgery or an accident.

exercises.prompt: Fill in έχω or με πονάει.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Έχω — Με πονάει — Έχω — Με πονάει — Έχω
Με πονάει το κεφάλι. — Έχω λίγο πυρετό. — Χρειάζομαι συνταγή; — Δύο φορές τη μέρα. — Χρειάζομαι γιατρό.
Με πονάει το κεφάλι μου. — Έχω λίγο πυρετό. — Χρειάζομαι ένα φάρμακο. — Δύο φορές τη μέρα, μετά το φαγητό. — Περαστικά!
